bipartite.kami_theme: The speaker, though feeling unworthy (おほけなく), declares that he covers/shelters the suffering people of this sorrowful world
bipartite.shimo_theme: The image of his black-dyed monastic sleeve spread over Mt. Hiei (the 'sooty-dyed sleeve' on the mountain where he 'stands/dwells as a woodcutter/monk')
bipartite.pivot_note: The kami-no-ku states the abstract religious vow (to shelter all beings under Buddhist compassion), and the shimo-no-ku reveals the concrete image that enacts it: the black sleeve of the monk's robe spread wide like a canopy over the mountain (Mt. Hiei, home of Tendai Buddhism) where he has taken his religious stand — the physical image of the sleeve becomes the visual manifestation of the abstract vow of universal protection.

kigo.note: 墨染の袖 (ink/soot-dyed sleeve) refers to the black robes of a Buddhist monk — this is not a seasonal image but a conventional religious/clothing image signaling renunciation of the world; the poem as a whole lacks a true seasonal anchor, as うき世 (sorrowful world) and そま (mountain forest/woodcutter) are moral-religious and toponymic images rather than seasonal ones

kakekotoba.interaction: うき世 primarily means 'this sorrowful/painful world' (憂き世), the standard Buddhist term for the transient world of suffering; the secondary sense of 浮き (floating, unstable) reinforces the image of an insecure, drifting existence that the speaker vows to shelter and stabilize

kakekotoba.reading_primary: 立つ (to stand, to take one's stand/position)
kakekotoba.interaction: わがたつそま literally means 'the mountain forest where I stand/take my place' (a conventional reference to Mt. Hiei, called 'waga tatsu soma' in the founding legend of the Tendai sect), while the cloth-cutting sense of たつ resonates with 袖 (sleeve) and 墨染 (dyed robe) in the final ku, activating a textile image network alongside the standing/place meaning

kakekotoba.reading_primary: 杣 (mountain forest / timberland, specifically Mt. Hiei by convention)
kakekotoba.reading_secondary: man who works the mountain forest (woodcutter, by extension the monk himself as one who labors in the 'forest' of religious practice)
kakekotoba.interaction: そま denotes both the literal wooded mountain (Mt. Hiei, site of the Tendai headquarters) and metaphorically the speaker's own place of ascetic labor, doubling the physical setting with the speaker's self-image as a humble laborer for the Buddhist Law

honkadori.source_poem: 阿耨多羅三藐三菩提の仏たち我が立つ杣に冥加あらせたまへ (Attributed to Saichō, founder of the Tendai sect, recorded in Shūi Wakashū and temple legend)
honkadori.function: Jien, as head of the Tendai sect (Sakino Daisojo), directly echoes Saichō's founding vow poem about Mt. Hiei ('the forest where I take my stand'), asserting his own inheritance of the founder's religious mission to protect and save all sentient beings from atop the same mountain
